q: What is the formula for Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG), and how do SAAG values ≥ 1.1 g/dL vs. < 1.1 g/dL differentiate ascites etiologies?
a:
SAAG = Serum Albumin − Ascitic Fluid Albumin.
• SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL: Indicates portal hypertension (e.g., Cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari syndrome, Congestive Heart Failure).
• SAAG < 1.1 g/dL: Indicates non-portal hypertension causes (e.g., Peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB peritonitis, Nephrotic syndrome, Pancreatic ascites).

q: How is Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP) diagnosed, and what are the initial treatment and prophylaxis guidelines?
a:
Diagnosis: Ascitic fluid absolute PMN count ≥ 250/mm3.
Treatment: Empiric 3rd generation cephalosporin (e.g., Cefotaxime or Ceftriaxone) plus IV Albumin (to prevent hepatorenal syndrome).
Prophylaxis: Daily Fluoroquinolone (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) or TMP-SMX.

q: What is the pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, and management of Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)?
a:
Pathophysiology: Severe splanchnic vasodilation leading to renal hypoperfusion and RAAS activation.
Diagnosis: Acute kidney injury in liver failure unresponsive to volume expansion (saline trial) with low urine Na+ (< 10 mEq/L) and normal renal ultrasound.
Management: Splanchnic vasoconstrictors (Terlipressin or Octreotide + Midodrine) + IV Albumin; definitive treatment is Liver Transplantation.

q: What lab parameters and initial fluid management strategies are critical in Acute Pancreatitis?
a:
Diagnosis: Serum Lipase ≥ 3× upper limit of normal (more specific than Amylase).
Severity/Hydration indicator: Rising BUN or Hct indicates intravascular depletion/hemoconcentration.
Initial Management: Aggressive fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's (LR) solution and enteral nutrition (if tolerated).

q: What genetic mutation, diagnostic findings, and treatment options characterize Wilson Disease?
a:
Mutation: AR mutation in ATP7B gene leading to impaired biliary copper secretion.
Clinical Presentation: Cirrhosis, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Labs: Low serum ceruloplasmin, increased 24-hr urinary Cu2+, increased hepatic copper content.
Treatment: Copper chelators (Penicillamine or Trientine) and oral Zinc.

q: What is the key diagnostic serologic marker and first-line therapy for Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)?
a:
Serology: Positive Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA).
Pathology: Autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic interlobular bile ducts (middle-aged women).
First-line therapy: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA); liver transplantation for end-stage disease.

q: What imaging finding, strong disease association, and major long-term risk are associated with Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)?
a:
Imaging (MRCP/ERCP): 'Bead-on-a-string' appearance (multifocal strictures and segmentally dilated intra/extrahepatic bile ducts).
Association: Strongly associated with Ulcerative Colitis (approx. 70-80%).
Complication: High risk of Cholangiocarcinoma.

q: What is the diagnostic gold standard for Achalasia, and what findings are expected on barium swallow and manometry?
a:
Barium swallow: Smooth taper of lower esophagus ('Bird's-beak' sign) with proximal dilation.
Esophageal Manometry (Gold standard): Absence of esophageal peristalsis and incomplete/absent relaxation of the Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES) with elevated resting LES pressure.

q: What is the anatomic defect in Zenker Diverticulum, how does it present, and what is the diagnostic test of choice?
a:
Anatomic location: Herniation through Killian triangle (between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles).
Presentation: Oropharyngeal dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, and a neck mass.
Diagnostic test: Barium esophagram (Upper endoscopy is contraindicated due to risk of perforation).

q: What is Boerhaave Syndrome, how is it diagnosed, and which contrast agent MUST be used?
a:
Definition: Transmural esophageal perforation following severe/repetitive vomiting.
Presentation: Retrosternal chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, and Hamman sign (mediastinal crunch).
Diagnosis: Esophagram using water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin). Barium contrast must be avoided due to risk of mediastinitis.

q: What is the management of early-stage gastric MALT Lymphoma associated with Helicobacter pylori?
a:
Management: H. pylori eradication therapy (e.g., PPI + Amoxicillin + Clarithromycin or Quadruple therapy).
Outcome: Complete regression of early low-grade MALT lymphoma occurs in up to 75-80% of cases following bacterial eradication alone.

q: What are the key serologic markers, small intestine biopsy findings, and malignancy risk associated with Celiac Disease?
a:
Serology: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) and IgA anti-endomysial antibodies.
Duodenal biopsy: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis.
Malignancy complication: Increased risk of Enteropathy-Associated T-Cell Lymphoma (EATL).

q: How do Crohn Disease and Ulcerative Colitis (UC) differ regarding gross/histologic distribution and transmural involvement?
a:
Crohn Disease: Transmural inflammation, skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas, cobblestoning, fistulas/perianal disease, ASCA positive.
Ulcerative Colitis: Mucosal/submucosal inflammation only, continuous extension starting from rectum, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps, p-ANCA positive.

q: What genetic defect causes Hereditary Hemochromatosis, what is the classic clinical triad, and what is the primary treatment?
a:
Genetics: AR mutation in HFE gene (e.g., C282Y mutation) leading to excessive iron absorption.
Classic triad: Cirrhosis, Diabetes mellitus ('bronze diabetes'), and Skin hyperpigmentation.
Treatment: Therapeutic phlebotomy (target serum ferritin < 50-100 ng/mL).

q: How does Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) differ from Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD) in terms of AST/ALT ratios?
a:
NAFLD/NASH: AST/ALT ratio is typically < 1 (ALT > AST). Associated with metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance.
Alcoholic Liver Disease: AST/ALT ratio is typically ≥ 2:1 (AST > ALT, with AST rarely > 500 U/L).

q: What are the first-line treatment regimens for initial episodes of Clostridioides difficile infection?
a:
First-line oral therapy: Oral Fidaxomicin (200 mg BID for 10 days) or Oral Vancomycin (125 mg QID for 10 days).
Note: IV Vancomycin is ineffective because it is not excreted into the intestinal lumen.

q: What is the classic presentation, initial best diagnostic test, and pathophysiology of Acute Mesenteric Ischemia?
a:
Pathophysiology: Sudden occlusion of the Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA), commonly from cardiac emboli (e.g., AFib).
Presentation: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings.
Initial best test: CT Angiography of the abdomen.

q: What is Angiodysplasia, what cardiac valvular disorder is it associated with, and how does it present?
a:
Definition: Vascular ectasia / tortuous submucosal veins commonly located in the cecum/right colon.
Association: Aortic Stenosis (Heyde syndrome, due to acquired von Willebrand factor cleavage) and renal disease.
Presentation: Episodic, painless lower GI bleeding (hematochezia) in elderly patients.

q: What is the mechanism of action of Lactulose and Rifaximin in treating Hepatic Encephalopathy?
a:
Lactulose: Colonic bacteria degrade lactulose into lactic acid and acetic acid → acidifies gut lumen → converts NH3 to non-absorbable NH4+ (ion trapping) + osmotic laxative effect.
Rifaximin: Non-absorbable antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria.

q: What is Ogilvie Syndrome (Acute Colonic Pseudo-obstruction), how is it diagnosed, and what pharmacological agent is used when conservative therapy fails?
a:
Definition: Massive dilation of the colon in the absence of mechanical obstruction, usually in severely ill/surgical patients.
Diagnosis: Abdominal CT showing marked colonic/cecal dilation without distal transition zone.
Pharmacotherapy: IV Neostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) if cecal diameter > 10-12 cm or failing conservative tx.
